items.title: Land at Izumo, settle into Matsue
items.tldr: Land at Izumo, transfer to Matsue, and catch the castle before sunset over Lake Shinji.
items.pace: Deliberately light: one transfer, one sight, an early dinner — the day absorbs arrival fatigue rather than fighting it.
items.body:
The airport limousine bus meets your flight and drops you in central Matsue in under an hour. Check in, then head for Matsue Castle — one of only twelve original castle keeps left in Japan, open to 17:00 in October (last entry 16:30). The donjon staircase gets genuinely congested with tour-bus arrivals roughly 10am–3pm; arriving right after opening or from ~16:30 is noticeably calmer, per multiple local visitor accounts.

The Matsue Lake Line loop bus (≈every 30 min, ¥250/ride or ¥700 all-day pass) links the station, the castle, the Horikawa boat dock, Shiomi Nawate, and Matsue Shinjiko Onsen — worth the pass if you'd rather not walk each leg with the group's 2 low-mobility travelers.

Walk the Shiomi Nawate samurai district along the castle moat afterward — low-key, mostly flat, and close enough to the castle that the two low-mobility travelers don't need a second transit leg. Tucked inside it, behind an unassuming long-gate next to the Lafcadio Hearn Old Residence, the small Tanabe Museum of Art is a quieter detour on the same block (9:00–17:00, last admission 16:30, ¥700 adult — its group rate needs 10 people, so a party of 8 pays individually).

Those two 16:30 cut-offs are the day's one real decision. The castle and the museum stop admitting at the same minute, so you can have the calm late-afternoon castle OR the museum, not both: if the group is checked in and at the castle gate by about 15:00, take the castle first and the museum after; land later than that and take the castle alone, then walk Shiomi Nawate at whatever pace the two slower walkers want. Marching eight people between two 16:30 deadlines on arrival day is exactly the kind of day this trip is meant not to have. End at Lake Shinji for sunset; it's one of Japan's more reliably photographed sunset spots, a 10-minute walk from most central Matsue hotels.

Dinner: Matsu-no-Daidokoro Konekkoya (2F of the Shinjiko Shijimikan, Chidori-cho; 0852-28-7511) for Shinjiko-shichin — the lake's "seven delicacies", shijimi clams, whitebait and eel among them. Dinner service runs 17:00–21:00 with last orders at 20:30, and its 24-seat banquet room is the one nearby room documented to hold all eight of you at one table; courses run ¥3,500 / ¥5,000 / ¥6,000. Phone ahead — the room is shared, not a buyout, and the smaller counter places along the lake can't take a group of 8 at all.
checklist: Confirm you're boarding the Matsue-route airport bus, not the Izumo-route one
Withdraw cash at a convenience-store ATM before the day is out

items.title: Izumo Taisha
items.tldr: A full day at Izumo Taisha — the shrine where, most years, the story is that all of Japan's gods gather every October.
items.pace: A round-trip day from Matsue on the Ichibata Railway; unhurried at the shrine, no reason to rush the return.
items.body:
The Ichibata Electric Railway runs directly from Matsue Shinjiko Onsen to Izumo Taisha-mae, with one same-platform transfer at Kawato — about an hour each way. Izumo Taisha itself is Japan's oldest and, to Shinto tradition, most important shrine after Ise; the grounds are open 6:00–19:00 and free to enter.

Worship here differently: it's two bows, four claps, one bow, not the two-clap pattern used almost everywhere else in Japan. The shrine's own explanation ties the fourth clap to the annual grand festival's eight claps, halved for everyday worship.

Many guides say October is "the month the gods gather at Izumo," but that's tied to the old lunar calendar, not the Gregorian one — in 2026 the Kamiari-zuki festival period actually falls November 9 to December 8, well after this trip. Nothing about the gathering happens during these dates; visit for the shrine itself, not for the festival.

Lunch: Tanakaya, five minutes from Izumo Taisha-mae Station, known for its three-color warigo soba. The more famous, 240-year-old Arakiya is closed on Wednesdays — worth knowing before walking over expecting it to be open.
constraints: Arakiya soba house closed Wednesdays — Tanakaya (open Wed) is the lunch pick this trip

items.title: Transfer to Omori, Iwami Ginzan
items.tldr: Check out of Matsue with the luggage, transfer to Omori, and ride the six-seat Ginzan Cart into the silver mine.
items.pace: The trip's one hard-timed day — a morning train with the luggage, a midday bus, a first-come shuttle, and a last bus out of the valley whose time you have to ask for on arrival.
items.body:
This is the day everything else on the trip is built around. Check out of Matsue with all luggage and take the JR San-in Line to Odashi (45–90 min depending on train) — IC cards stop working at Izumo-shi Station, so have cash or a paper ticket ready before boarding the second leg. From Odashi, the Iwami Kotsu community bus reaches the Iwami Ginzan World Heritage Center in about 30 minutes — but the centre is not the village: the operator puts it roughly five minutes by road from the Omori townscape, with another bus leg in between. Check which stop your service actually terminates at before you load eight people and the luggage onto it, and drop bags at your Omori lodging first if it's on the way.

Iwami Ginzan is a UNESCO World Heritage silver-mining town — Edo-period merchant houses lining a river valley, with the actual mine tunnel (Ryugenji Mabu) 2.3 km up the valley. Private cars are banned past the park entrance, so the only way in besides walking is the Ginzan Cart: a 6-seat electric shuttle, no reservations, first-come first-served, {{fact:ginzan-cart-500-yen}} depending on where you board. The operator publishes 12–14 runs a day between 8:00 and 18:00 and no fixed interval, so the honest planning number is up to an hour to the next cart, not half an hour. With a party of 8 (two with limited walking tolerance), that means two loads minimum and a second group left standing — decide at the stop who waits and who walks, rather than discovering the split when the cart pulls away with six. If the cart is full, not running, or the weather's turned, the walk is 2.3 km / ≈45 minutes each way on an unpaved forest trail — a rental e-bike ({{fact:iwami-ginzan-ebike-700-yen}} for 2hr, from Rentacycle Kawamura by the Daikansho-mae plaza) is a third, confirmed option for anyone who'd rather not wait out a cart cycle or walk the whole way; the operator recommends the electric bikes over ordinary ones because the valley road climbs. Local bus service into Omori itself runs on limited frequency — the operator's own guidance is to check the timetable ahead and allow at least half a day for the site.

The deadline that ends this day is the last bus out of the valley, not a train — you checked out of Matsue this morning and you are sleeping on this side tonight, so nothing here depends on catching a JR service back east. What you can miss is the last Iwami Kotsu bus from Omori / the World Heritage Center toward Ota-shi and your Oda base, and the cart's own 18:00 close is not that deadline. ⚠ Iwami Kotsu revises this timetable seasonally and doesn't publish it on the World Heritage Center's site — ask at the centre's information desk the moment you arrive, and write the last departure down. If it goes: the centre's own transport page lists the Ota-shi taxi firms, Fuji Daiichi Kotsu (0854-82-0660) and Nihon Kotsu's Ota office (0854-82-0456) — a party of 8 is two or three cars, so call before the last bus leaves, not after.

Lunch or an afternoon coffee: Gungendo's main store café, a 170-year-old renovated merchant house in the townscape (closed Wednesdays — no conflict today).
checklist: Cash on hand before Izumo-shi Station (IC cards stop working past it)
Confirm Omori lodging can hold the whole party of 8 across its buildings
Ask the World Heritage Center desk for today's last bus toward Ota-shi on arrival, and note the taxi numbers
constraints: Ginzan Cart: no reservations, 6-seat capacity, 12–14 runs a day (no fixed interval), can suspend without notice in bad weather
Last Iwami Kotsu bus out of Omori toward Ota-shi — seasonal timetable, confirm it on arrival

plan_b.body: The Ginzan Cart can suspend in bad weather with no notice, and the 2.3km trail alternative isn't reasonable in a downpour with the group's mobility mix. In the village itself, Gungendo's main store — a covered merchant house with its courtyard café — is the dry stop that needs no transit at all. The indoor Iwami Ginzan World Heritage Center is the bigger wet-weather option, but it is NOT at the townscape entrance: the operator puts it about five minutes by road away, so it costs a bus each way and a wait at each end. Check the return time before you commit to it in the rain, or the fallback becomes its own problem.

items.title: Omori morning, fly out of Izumo
items.tldr: A slow Omori morning, then the return chain east to fly out of Izumo Airport.
items.pace: No fixed sight this morning — protect it for the group's slower walkers, then start the return chain by early afternoon.
items.body:
Leave the morning unscheduled: a second, quieter pass through the Omori townscape, or simply breakfast without a transit deadline. This is the trip's built-in slack for anyone who found Thursday's mine day tiring.

From early afternoon, reverse the transfer: Iwami Kotsu bus to Odashi, JR back to Izumo-shi (re-entering IC coverage), then the airport limousine bus or a taxi for the final stretch to Izumo Airport — there's no direct rail link into the terminal.
